facts.fact: The Guptas rose on the ruins of the Kushana (north) and Satavahana (Deccan) empires.
The Guptas kept North India united c. 240–550 CE.
The Gupta empire was smaller than the Mauryan empire.
The Guptas were originally feudatories of the Kushanas.
The Gupta base was Magadha (Bihar), later eastern U.P.
Gupta wealth drew on central Indian/south Bihar iron ore and Byzantine silk trade.
The Vallabhi era is identical to the Gupta era.
The Gupta era begins 319–320 CE, credited to Chandragupta I.
Pataliputra, Prayag and Ujjain were the key Gupta cities.
Sri Gupta (c. 240–280 CE) founded the dynasty.
Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha used the title 'Maharaja'.
The Poona copper plate of Prabhavatigupta calls Sri Gupta 'Adhiraja'.
The early Gupta home may have been north or central Bengal.
Ghatotkacha (280–319 CE), son of Sri Gupta, had a peaceful reign.
Chandragupta I first took the title 'Maharajadhiraja'.
Chandragupta I married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi.
The Lichchhavis were headquartered at Vaishali.
Chandragupta I ruled 319/320–335 CE.
Chandragupta I ruled Ayodhya, Prayaga and Magadha.
The King-and-Queen (Kumaradevi) gold coin marks the Lichchhavi alliance.
Samudragupta is called the 'Napoleon of India' (V. A. Smith).
Samudragupta ruled c. 335–375/380 CE.
Samudragupta followed a policy of blood and iron.
The Allahabad (Prayag) Prashasti was composed by Harishena.
Samudragupta's title was 'Kaviraja' (King of Poets).
His coins show him playing the veena.
Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha.
He received tribute from Assam, Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.
Aryavarta kings were uprooted and annexed (prasabhoddharana).
Dakshinapatha kings were captured, released and reinstated (grahana–moksha–anugraha).
Twelve southern kings are listed in the Prashasti.
Southern kings included Hastivarman of Vengi, Mahendragiri of Pishtapura and Kubera of Devarashtra (Andhra).
Vishnugopa of Kanchi (Pallava) was among the southern kings.
Atavika (forest) kings were made servants.
Frontier kingdoms (Samatata, Kamarupa, Nepal) paid tribute.
Meghavarman of Sri Lanka sought leave to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.
Harishena was Sandhivigrahika (minister of peace and war) and Kumaramatya.
The Prashasti is carved on an Ashokan pillar, in Sanskrit champu style.
Samudragupta left an inscription at Eran (M.P.).
Samudragupta issued archer, tiger-slayer, Ashvamedha and veena coins.
Chandragupta II took the title 'Vikramaditya'.
Chandragupta II was also Simhavikrama.
Chandragupta II defeated the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas), winning Malwa and Gujarat.
His empire ran from the Indus to Bengal and the Himalayas to the Narmada.
His daughter Prabhavatigupta was a Vakataka queen.
Fa-Hien visited India in the reign of Chandragupta II.
Chandragupta II patronised the Navaratnas (nine gems).
Devichandraguptam tells that Chandragupta II killed the Shaka king and Ramagupta and married Dhruvadevi.
Ujjain was the second capital of Chandragupta II.
Chandragupta II took the title 'Paramabhagavata'.
The Udayagiri caves (Vidisha) with the Varaha relief belong to his reign.
Chandragupta II began Gupta silver coinage after conquering the Western Kshatrapas.
Dhanvantari, a physician, was one of the Navaratnas.
The Mehrauli Iron Pillar carries the inscription of Chandragupta II.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq later moved it to Delhi.
The pillar's rust-resistance shows advanced Gupta metallurgy.
Fa-Hien came c. 399 CE via China, the Gobi and Central Asia.
Fa-Hien described a peaceful, law-abiding, vegetarian society with no spy system.
Fa-Hien noted the bad condition of the outcastes.
Fa-Hien came to collect Vinaya texts; his account is the Fo-kuo-ki.
Fa-Hien does not name the reigning king.
Chandalas lived outside towns and struck wood to announce themselves.
Nalanda emerged under Kumaragupta I.
Nalanda peaked under Harshavardhana and the Palas.
Nalanda taught mainly Mahayana Buddhism and shaped Tibetan Buddhism.
Taxila taught political science, medicine and military tactics; alumni Chanakya and Charaka.
Kumaragupta I bore the titles Shakraditya and Mahendraditya.
Kumaragupta I ruled 415–455 CE.
Kumaragupta I performed the Ashvamedha.
Kumaragupta I's peacock coins show Kartikeya.
There is little evidence of Kumaragupta I's military achievements.
Skandagupta fought the earliest Huna invasions.
Skandagupta repaired the Sudarshan Lake.
The Bhitari pillar inscription (Ghazipur) belongs to Skandagupta (wars with Pushyamitras and Hunas).
Skandagupta's Junagadh inscription records the repair by Chakrapalita, son of governor Parnadatta.
Skandagupta also took the title 'Vikramaditya'.
Skandagupta ruled 455–467 CE.
Vishnugupta (c. 540–550 CE) was the last known Gupta ruler.
Purugupta, Kumaragupta II and Buddhagupta ruled during the decline.
Narasimhagupta (Baladitya) fought the Hunas under Mihirakula.
Toramana was the Huna chief who conquered western and central India; Mihirakula was his son.
Yashodharman of Malwa defeated Mihirakula (Mandsaur inscription).
Mihirakula's capital was Sakala (Sialkot); he persecuted Buddhists.
The Eran inscription of Bhanugupta (510 CE) is the first record of Sati.
Weak later kings and over-mighty governors (feudalism) weakened the empire.
Huna invasions from the north-west were a major cause of decline.
The Pushyabhutis (Thanesar) were a successor state.
The Pratiharas were based at Kannauj.
The land-revenue system strengthened provincial governors (e.g. Aulikaras).
Bhukti was the province, under an Uparika.
Vishaya was the district, under a Vishayapati.
In eastern India Vishayas were divided into Vithis.
Village headmen became important in Gupta times.
Salaries were first paid in cash, later replaced by land grants (source text).
Gupta administration was less centralised than the Mauryan; feudal tendencies grew.
Shrenis were self-governing guilds of artisans and merchants.
Vidisha's ivory-carvers' guild funded Sanchi's southern gateway.
Guild seals from Vaishali and Bhita show the guilds flourished.
District boards had the Nagarashreshthi, Sarthavaha, Prathama Kulika and Prathama Kayastha.
Kumaramatyas were a cadre of high officers.
Bhaga was the king's share of the produce (usually one-sixth).
Hiranya was a tax paid in cash.
Halivakara was a plough tax.
Udakabhaga was a water tax.
Vishti was forced labour.
Uparikara was an extra tax on all subjects.
Bhoga was periodic supplies of fruit, firewood and flowers to the king.
Agrahara grants to Brahmanas were perpetual, hereditary and tax-free.
The Narada Smriti (5th century) lists Brahmana privileges.
Land classes: Kshetra, Khila, Aprahata, Vasti, Gopata Sarah.
Sea trade went to Suvarnabhumi (Burma), Yavadvipa (Java) and Kamboja (Cambodia).
Gupta ports: Tamralipti, Broach, Sopara, Kalyan.
Northern trade declined due to floods and Huna attacks.
The Gupta kings were Vaishnavas.
The Gupta royal emblem was Garuda.
Bhagavatism spread the idea of avatars (incarnations of Vishnu).
Brahmins became the dominant, wealthy section through land grants.
Shudras could now hear the epics and Puranas and worship Krishna.
Caste was by birth; inter-caste marriages declined.
Women were denied education; polygamy and the Devadasi system existed.
Gupta gold coins were called 'Dinaras'.
Gupta coin types also include a reclining-lion type.
The Kushanas issued the purest gold coins; the Guptas the most numerous.
The Gupta age is called the 'Golden Age of India'.
Aryabhata gave the decimal place-value system and the concept of zero.
Aryabhata stated the earth rotates on its axis.
Aryabhata's work is the Aryabhatiya.
The Aryabhatiya was written in 499 CE at Kusumapura.
Aryabhata explained eclipses by the shadows of the earth and moon.
Varahamihira wrote the Panchasiddhantika (505 CE).
The five siddhantas: Surya, Romaka, Paulisa, Vasishtha, Paitamaha.
The Romaka Siddhanta shows Greek/Roman influence.
Varahamihira wrote the Brihat Samhita.
Brahmagupta (Brahmasphuta Siddhanta) came later, in the 7th century.
Palakapya wrote the Hastyayurveda (elephant medicine).
Ajanta and Ellora caves hold the finest murals of the age.
The Sultanganj Buddha is a ~7.5 ft copper figure (Gupta–Pala).
The Gupta period began free-standing temple architecture.
Nagara (north): shikhara, Panchayatan — Dashavatara temple, Deogarh.
Dravidian (south): vimana, high walls; flourished under the Cholas.
Vesara: hybrid of Nagara and Dravidian (Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas).
Bhitargaon (Kanpur) is an early brick temple.
Sanchi Temple 17 is an early flat-roofed temple.
Tigawa and Nachna have other early Gupta temples.
Ajanta murals are mostly Vakataka-patronised.
The Allahabad pillar carries Samudragupta's inscription.
Kalidasa wrote Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha and Kumarasambhava.
Vishakhadatta wrote the Mudrarakshasa.
Vishakhadatta also wrote the Devichandraguptam.
Shudraka wrote the Mrichchhakatika.
Mrichchhakatika means 'The Little Clay Cart' (Charudatta and Vasantasena).
Amarasimha compiled the Amarakosha.
Bhasa wrote thirteen plays, including Svapnavasavadatta.
Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram has the Sunga prince Agnimitra as hero.
Kalidasa also wrote the Ritusamhara.
The Panchatantra (Vishnu Sharma) is usually placed in this age.
The Puranas were compiled and revised; secular literature flourished.
Sanskrit grammar developed on the basis of Panini and Patanjali.
Vatsyayana wrote the Nyaya Bhashya.
